customLessons.title: Properties and Uses of Materials
objectives: Identify different materials used in common everyday objects (wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, rubber).
Describe observable physical properties including hardness, flexibility, texture, and absorbency.
Match everyday materials with their practical functions and explain why specific materials are chosen.
customLessons.content:
Materials are substances used to make objects. Everyday items are made from materials like wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper, fabric, and rubber.

Each material has distinct physical properties. Hard materials like iron and hardwood resist scratching. Flexible materials like rubber and silicone bend easily without breaking. Absorbent materials like cotton and sponges soak up liquids, while waterproof materials like plastic and glass repel water.

Choosing the right material depends on its purpose. For example, cooking pots are made of metal because metal conducts heat and does not melt easily, while the handles are made of plastic or wood to protect our hands from burns.

slides.title: Properties and Uses of Materials
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 1 Science

Discover how the properties of wood, metal, plastic, glass, and rubber shape our everyday world.

slides.title: Common Materials Around Us
slides.content:
Look around your classroom and home:
• Wood: Desks, doors, and pencils (sturdy, natural)
• Metal: Nails, spoons, and coins (hard, shiny, strong)
• Plastic: Bottles, rulers, and lunchboxes (lightweight, waterproof)
• Glass: Windows, mirrors, and spectacles (transparent, smooth)
• Fabric & Rubber: Clothes, tires, and erasers (soft, flexible, elastic)

slides.title: Observing Physical Properties
slides.content:
How can we describe materials?
1. Hardness: Can it resist scratching? (Diamond vs Chalk)
2. Flexibility: Can it bend without breaking? (Rubber vs Ceramic)
3. Absorbency: Can it soak up water? (Sponge vs Plastic wrap)
4. Transparency: Can light pass through it? (Clear glass vs Wood)
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Observe color and texture
Step 2: Test flexibility by gentle bending
Step 3: Test absorbency with water droplet
Step 4: Record findings in science notebook

slides.title: Matching Materials to Their Purpose
slides.content:
Why are cooking pots made of metal while their handles are made of plastic or wood?

• Metal conducts heat quickly to cook food evenly.
• Plastic and wood are thermal insulators that stay cool, preventing burns when lifting the pot!

slides.title: Classroom Quick Check
slides.content:
Which material would be the best choice for making a rain umbrella?
A) Cotton fabric
B) Waterproof plastic
C) Thick cardboard
D) Heavy iron

Correct Answer: B (Waterproof plastic keeps rain out and is lightweight!)

customLessons.title: Changes in Materials and Environmental Responsibility
objectives: Describe physical changes in materials when bent, pressed, hammered, or cut.
Observe and describe the effects of heating and cooling on common substances.
Practice the 5Rs of waste management (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Repair, Refuse) to care for the environment.
customLessons.content:
Materials can change in size, shape, or state without forming new substances. Cutting paper, bending a wire, pressing clay, or hammering an aluminum can changes how they look, but the material remains the same.

Heating and cooling cause noticeable changes. Heat melts solid ice into liquid water and softens candle wax. Cooling water in a freezer turns it back into solid ice.

Improper disposal of materials pollutes the land, rivers, and oceans. Practicing the 5Rs—Reduce waste, Reuse containers, Recycle paper and plastics, Repair broken items, and Refuse single-use plastics—keeps our community clean and protects wildlife.

slides.title: Changes in Materials & Environmental Care
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 1 Science

Learn how materials change shape, size, and state, and how we can protect our surroundings.

slides.title: Physical Actions on Materials
slides.content:
How can we change materials without creating new substances?
• Bending: Soft metal wire or rubber bends easily
• Pressing: Modeling clay changes shape under finger pressure
• Hammering: Flattening metal sheets or soda cans
• Cutting: Scissors slicing paper or cloth into smaller pieces

slides.title: Temperature: Heating and Cooling
slides.content:
Thermal changes in everyday life:
• Heating ice: Solid ice melts into liquid water
• Heating wax: Solid candle wax softens and turns into liquid
• Cooling water: Liquid water freezes into solid ice at 0°C
• Cooling wax: Liquid wax hardens back into a solid block
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Place ice cube in sun
Step 2: Observe melting into water
Step 3: Place water in freezer
Step 4: Observe refreezing into ice

slides.title: The 5Rs of Environmental Responsibility
slides.content:
Protecting our community and planet:
1. Reduce: Use less disposable packaging
2. Reuse: Refill water bottles and jars
3. Recycle: Turn paper and plastic into new goods
4. Repair: Fix broken school bags and shoes
5. Refuse: Say no to single-use plastic bags and straws

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Protecting Our Planet
slides.content:
Which action shows the "Reuse" practice of the 5Rs?
A) Throwing old plastic bottles into the river
B) Turning an old glass peanut butter jar into a pencil holder
C) Burning dried leaves and plastic wrappers
D) Buying a new plastic bag every day

Correct Answer: B (Repurposing containers gives them new life!)

customLessons.title: Earth Materials and Their Uses
objectives: Identify common Earth materials such as soil, rocks, sand, water, and minerals.
Compare the characteristics of different soil types (clay, sand, loam).
Explain how living things rely on Earth materials for food, shelter, and construction.
customLessons.content:
The Earth provides natural materials that support all living things. These include rocks, minerals, water, and different types of soil.

Soil is formed from broken rocks and decayed plant and animal matter. Sand has large, gritty particles that drain water quickly. Clay has tiny, sticky particles that hold a lot of water. Loam is a balanced mixture of sand, clay, and rich organic humus, making it the best soil for growing crops and garden plants.

Rocks and minerals are quarried for building roads, houses, bridges, and tools. Water from rivers and underground springs provides drinking water and nourishes agricultural crops.

slides.title: Earth Materials and Their Uses
slides.content:
Grade 3 — Term 3 Science

Discover the natural resources beneath our feet: rocks, minerals, water, and fertile soil.

slides.title: Earth's Natural Treasures
slides.content:
Our planet provides essential raw materials:
• Rocks & Minerals: Basalt, limestone, granite, quartz
• Soil: The loose upper layer of Earth\'s surface
• Water: Streams, rivers, lakes, and aquifers
• Fossil Fuels & Ores: Energy and metals

slides.title: Comparing the Three Main Soil Types
slides.content:
Characteristics of soils:
• Sand: Large, rough, gritty particles; water drains very quickly
• Clay: Very fine, smooth particles; holds lots of water and becomes sticky
• Loam: Balanced mix of sand, silt, clay, and rich organic humus; holds moisture while draining well
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Feel soil texture with fingers
Step 2: Pour 100mL water over each soil
Step 3: Measure drainage time
Step 4: Check organic plant growth

slides.title: Practical Uses in Society
slides.content:
How we use Earth materials:
• Construction: Gravel, sand, and cement build roads, bridges, and school buildings
• Agriculture: Loam soil grows rice, corn, fruits, and vegetables
• Ceramics: Clay is molded and baked into bricks, flowerpots, and roof tiles
• Daily Life: Natural water sustains health and sanitation

slides.title: Quick Quiz: The Best Soil
slides.content:
Which soil type is dark, nutrient-rich, and best for planting vegetables in school gardens?
A) Pure dry sand
B) Sticky dense clay
C) Rich organic loam
D) Crushed volcanic rock

Correct Answer: C (Loam holds the right balance of water, air, and nutrients!)

customLessons.title: Physical Properties of Materials
objectives: Classify materials based on whether they absorb water, float or sink, and conduct heat or electricity.
Relate density to the floating and sinking behavior of materials in liquids.
Identify conductors and insulators of heat and electricity in household items.
customLessons.content:
Materials possess distinct physical properties that can be observed and measured without altering their chemical makeup.

Density determines whether an object floats or sinks: objects with lower density than water float (wood, cork, oil), while objects denser than water sink (iron nails, stones). Porous materials like sponges and cotton towels absorb water into internal pores, whereas non-porous materials like plastics and metals shed water.

Thermal and electrical conductivity are vital properties: metals like copper and aluminum are good conductors that transfer heat and electricity quickly. Insulators like rubber, wood, and plastic resist the flow of heat and electric current, keeping us safe.

slides.title: Physical Properties of Materials
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Term 1 Science

Explore density, floating vs sinking, absorbency, and thermal and electrical conductivity.

slides.title: Floating vs Sinking: Density Explained
slides.content:
Why does a giant steel ship float while a small iron nail sinks?

• Density is mass divided by volume (d = m/V).
• Water has a density of 1.0 g/cm³.
• Objects denser than water sink (iron: 7.8 g/cm³).
• Ships have hollow hulls filled with air, making their average density lower than water!

slides.title: Absorbency and Porosity
slides.content:
Porous vs Non-porous materials:
• Absorbent: Cotton, paper towels, sponge (have tiny pores that draw water in by capillary action)
• Non-absorbent: Glass, plastic wrap, aluminum foil (smooth, sealed surfaces that repel water)
• Application: Diapers and bandages use absorbent fibers, while raincoats use non-porous vinyl.
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Submerge sponge in water
Step 2: Measure absorbed water mass
Step 3: Submerge plastic sheet
Step 4: Compare water retention

slides.title: Conductors vs Insulators
slides.content:
Managing Heat and Electricity:
• Electrical Conductors: Copper, silver, aluminum, brass (electrons move freely)
• Electrical Insulators: Rubber, plastic, dry wood, glass (block electric flow)
• Thermal Conductors: Aluminum pots heat food fast
• Thermal Insulators: Styrofoam and silicone prevent heat transfer

slides.title: Classroom Investigation Check
slides.content:
Why are power cords wrapped in rubber or plastic coating?
A) To make the cord look colorful
B) Because rubber is an electrical insulator that protects users from electric shocks
C) To make electricity travel faster
D) Because plastic generates electrical current

Correct Answer: B (Insulation ensures safety!)

customLessons.title: Chemical Properties of Materials
objectives: Describe chemical properties of materials such as flammability, reactivity with oxygen (rusting), and biodegradability.
Differentiate biodegradable materials from non-biodegradable materials based on decomposition.
Identify chemical warning symbols and safety precautions when handling reactive or hazardous substances.
customLessons.content:
Chemical properties describe a material's potential to undergo chemical reactions and transform into new substances.

Flammability is the ability of a material to burn in the presence of oxygen, such as dry wood, paper, and kerosene. Rusting (corrosion) occurs when iron reacts with moisture and oxygen over time to produce iron oxide (rust).

Biodegradability refers to whether natural microorganisms can decompose materials into harmless organic matter. Banana peels and leaves biodegrade within weeks, while synthetic plastics and Styrofoam persist in landfills and oceans for centuries.

Chemical hazard pictograms warn against flammable, corrosive, toxic, and explosive hazards on chemical containers.

slides.title: Chemical Properties of Materials
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Term 1 Science

Investigate flammability, rusting, biodegradability, and safe handling of reactive materials.

slides.title: Flammability & Reactivity with Oxygen
slides.content:
Key Chemical Behaviors:
• Flammability: How easily a substance ignites and burns (e.g., alcohol, dry wood, paper, gasoline)
• Corrosion & Rusting: Iron combines with oxygen and moisture to form reddish-brown iron oxide
• Oxidation weakens metal structures over time!

slides.title: Biodegradable vs Non-Biodegradable
slides.content:
Decomposition by natural microorganisms:
• Biodegradable: Fruit peelings (2 weeks), paper (2 months), cotton (5 months) — breakdown into organic soil nutrients
• Non-Biodegradable: Aluminum cans (200 years), plastic bottles (450 years), Styrofoam (never breaks down fully, turns into microplastics)
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Bury organic peel in soil
Step 2: Bury plastic wrapper beside it
Step 3: Check after 4 weeks
Step 4: Record decomposition rates

slides.title: Chemical Safety & Warning Labels
slides.content:
Reading hazard symbols:
• Flame symbol: Highly flammable; keep away from heat sources
• Skull and crossbones: Toxic/poisonous if swallowed or inhaled
• Corrosive symbol: Causes burns to skin and eyes; wear gloves
• Exclamation mark: Harmful irritant

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Preventing Rust
slides.content:
Why are iron fences, gates, and bicycle frames painted?
A) Only to make them look shiny
B) Paint creates a barrier that blocks moisture and oxygen from touching the iron
C) Paint makes the iron lighter
D) Paint causes iron to turn into copper

Correct Answer: B (Airtight barrier prevents chemical rusting!)

customLessons.title: Effect of Temperature on Materials
objectives: Explain how changes in temperature alter the physical state, volume, and shape of materials.
Describe phase changes including melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation, and sublimation.
Relate thermal expansion and contraction to real-life applications like thermometers and bridges.
customLessons.content:
Temperature measures the average thermal kinetic energy of particles in a material. Adding heat speeds up particles and pushes them apart, causing thermal expansion. Removing heat slows particles down and brings them closer, causing thermal contraction.

Phase changes occur at specific temperatures: heating solid ice turns it into liquid water (melting); boiling liquid water creates water vapor (evaporation); cooling water vapor turns it back to liquid (condensation); freezing liquid turns it into solid ice.

Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without becoming a liquid (e.g., mothballs or dry ice).

Engineers leave expansion joints in concrete bridges and railway tracks so materials can expand on hot days without buckling or cracking.

slides.title: Effect of Temperature on Materials
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Term 1 Science

Discover how heat transforms solids, liquids, and gases and causes materials to expand and contract.

slides.title: Thermal Expansion & Contraction
slides.content:
What happens to atoms when heated?
• Adding heat: Particles gain kinetic energy, vibrate faster, and spread apart (Expansion)
• Removing heat: Particles lose energy, move closer together (Contraction)
• Thermometers work on expansion: heating the bulb expands the liquid up the tube!

slides.title: The Five Key Phase Changes
slides.content:
Transitions between states:
1. Melting: Solid -> Liquid (Ice to water at 0°C)
2. Freezing: Liquid -> Solid (Water to ice at 0°C)
3. Evaporation: Liquid -> Gas (Water boiling to steam at 100°C)
4. Condensation: Gas -> Liquid (Steam cooling into water droplets)
5. Sublimation: Solid -> Gas directly (Dry ice, naphthalene balls)
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Solid (particles vibrate in place)
Step 2: Add heat -> Melting
Step 3: Liquid (particles flow)
Step 4: Add heat -> Evaporation (gas freely expands)

slides.title: Engineering for Heat: Expansion Joints
slides.content:
Why are there small gaps in bridges, railway tracks, and highway roads?

• On hot sunny days, steel and concrete expand.
• Without expansion joints, railway tracks would bend and buckle dangerously!
• The gaps give materials room to expand safely.

slides.title: Classroom Thinking Challenge
slides.content:
Why do water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass of iced water on a warm day?
A) The water leaked through the solid glass
B) Invisible water vapor in the warm air cooled down upon touching the cold glass and condensed
C) The glass melted slightly
D) The cold generated water from glass molecules

Correct Answer: B (Condensation of water vapor from the surrounding air!)

customLessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
objectives: Distinguish between physical changes (reversible, no new substance) and chemical changes (irreversible, new substance formed).
Identify evidence of chemical change: release of gas, color change, temperature change, light emission, or formation of a precipitate.
Classify common household and kitchen processes as physical or chemical changes.
customLessons.content:
A physical change alters only the physical appearance, size, shape, or state of matter, while the chemical identity stays identical. Examples: chopping wood, shredding paper, melting ice, dissolving sugar in water.

A chemical change occurs when bonds break and atoms rearrange to form entirely new chemical substances with different properties. Examples: burning firewood to ash, baking a cake, souring milk, rusting iron.

Key indicators of a chemical change include: bubbling/gas production, unexpected color change, temperature change (becoming hot or cold without external heating), light emission, or odor change.

slides.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Term 1 Science

Learn to spot the crucial difference between changes in appearance and the birth of new substances.

slides.title: Physical Change: Same Identity
slides.content:
Characteristics of Physical Change:
• Alters only size, shape, or state
• No new substance is created
• Often easily reversible
• Examples: Cutting paper, melting butter, dissolving salt in water, crushing an aluminum can

slides.title: Chemical Change: New Substances Formed
slides.content:
Characteristics of Chemical Change:
• Chemical bonds break and new bonds form
• New substance has completely different properties
• Difficult or impossible to reverse
• Examples: Burning wood (produces ash and smoke), rusting nails, baking a cake, milk souring
slides.mediaUrl:
Sign 1: Gas bubbles formed (effervescence)
Sign 2: Unexpected color shift
Sign 3: Heat/Light produced
Sign 4: Odor released
Sign 5: Solid precipitate formed

slides.title: Kitchen Science Comparison
slides.content:
Spot the difference in the kitchen:
• Dissolving sugar in hot water -> Physical Change (sugar can be recovered by boiling water away)
• Caramelizing sugar into brown syrup -> Chemical Change (heat breaks sugar molecules into caramel)
• Freezing fruit juice -> Physical Change
• Cooking an egg -> Chemical Change (proteins denature permanently)

slides.title: Check for Understanding
slides.content:
When vinegar is mixed with baking soda, rapid fizzing bubbles appear and the beaker cools down. What happened?
A) A physical change where vinegar boiled
B) A chemical change because carbon dioxide gas was created by a reaction
C) The baking soda simply melted
D) No change took place

Correct Answer: B (Gas bubbles and temperature drop prove a chemical reaction!)

customLessons.title: Responsible Use and Management of Materials
objectives: Practice safe handling, storage, and disposal of toxic, flammable, and corrosive household chemicals.
Apply 4-way waste segregation (biodegradable, non-biodegradable, recyclable, hazardous) in school and home.
Advocate for sustainable consumption, zero-waste initiatives, and environmental stewardship.
customLessons.content:
Modern life utilizes diverse chemical products (bleach, pesticides, detergents, batteries, paints). Using them safely protects human health and the natural environment.

Safety rules: Keep chemicals in their original labeled containers, store out of reach of young children, wear gloves and face masks when handling irritants, and never mix household cleaners like bleach and ammonia.

Waste segregation: Separate wet organic waste (food scraps for composting) from dry recyclables (paper, plastic, glass bottles) and hazardous household waste (spent batteries, expired medicines, fluorescent bulbs).

Practicing environmental stewardship keeps Philippine communities clean, prevents flooding caused by plastic-clogged drainage canals, and protects marine biodiversity.

slides.title: Responsible Use & Management of Materials
slides.content:
Grade 4 — Term 1 Science

Safety protocols for household chemicals, 4-way waste segregation, and community sustainability.

slides.title: Hazardous Household Chemicals
slides.content:
Common chemicals requiring care:
• Bleach & Disinfectants: Strong oxidizers; irritate skin and lungs
• Pesticides & Insect Sprays: Toxic chemicals; avoid inhalation
• Paints, Thinner, & Gasoline: Highly flammable volatile compounds
• Spent Batteries & Fluorescent Bulbs: Contain heavy metals (mercury, lead, cadmium)

slides.title: Core Safety Rules for Chemical Use
slides.content:
Always follow these safety steps:
1. Keep in original containers with clear labels
2. Never mix bleach with ammonia or acids (releases lethal chloramine gas!)
3. Store in locked cabinets away from food and children
4. Wear protective rubber gloves and open windows for ventilation
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Read label warnings
Step 2: Wear protective mask & gloves
Step 3: Use exact recommended amount
Step 4: Dispose of container properly

slides.title: 4-Way Waste Segregation at School
slides.content:
Sorting waste properly:
• Green Bin (Biodegradable): Food scraps, fruit peelings, dried leaves -> Composting
• Blue Bin (Recyclables): Paper, cardboard, PET bottles, tin cans -> Recycling plants
• Black Bin (Residual Waste): Styrofoam, soiled wrappers -> Sanitary landfills
• Red/Yellow Bin (Special Hazardous): Batteries, aerosol cans, expired medicines

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Safety in the Home
slides.content:
Why should household cleaning chemicals never be transferred into empty soft drink bottles?
A) It makes the chemicals lose their cleaning power
B) Someone might mistake the chemical for a beverage and drink it, causing severe poisoning
C) Soft drink bottles make chemicals freeze
D) Plastic makes bleach evaporate immediately

Correct Answer: B (Accidental ingestion prevention is critical!)

customLessons.title: Properties of Matter
objectives: Differentiate intensive properties (density, boiling point, hardness) from extensive properties (mass, volume, length).
Measure and calculate mass, volume, and density (d = m/V) using laboratory instruments.
Explain why intensive properties are essential for identifying unknown materials and substances.
customLessons.content:
Matter is defined by physical and chemical properties that can be quantified and compared.

Extensive properties depend on the amount of matter in a sample. Examples include mass (grams), volume (milliliters/cubic centimeters), and length. If you double the amount of water, its mass and volume double.

Intensive properties do NOT depend on the amount of matter. Examples include density, boiling point, melting point, color, and electrical conductivity. 1 drop of pure water and 1 gallon of pure water both have a density of 1.0 g/cm³ and boil at 100°C at sea level.

Calculating density (d = mass / volume) allows scientists to identify unknown minerals and materials accurately.

slides.title: Properties of Matter
slides.content:
Grade 5 — Term 1 Science

Master the distinction between extensive and intensive properties and calculate density (d = m/V).

slides.title: Extensive vs Intensive Properties
slides.content:
Comparing the two property classes:
• Extensive Properties: Depend on sample size
  - Mass (g, kg)
  - Volume (mL, cm³)
  - Length & Total Energy
• Intensive Properties: Independent of sample size
  - Density (1.0 g/cm³ for water)
  - Boiling point (100°C for water)
  - Color, Odor, Hardness, and Conductivity

slides.title: The Density Formula in Practice
slides.content:
Formula: d = m / V (Density = Mass ÷ Volume)

• Mass is measured using a beam balance or electronic digital scale (grams).
• Volume is measured using a graduated cylinder via liquid displacement:
  V_object = V_final - V_initial
• Units: g/cm³ (for solids) or g/mL (for liquids).
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Weigh sample on digital scale (m)
Step 2: Fill graduated cylinder to 50mL
Step 3: Submerge object, record new level (V)
Step 4: Divide mass by volume (d = m/V)

slides.title: Laboratory Mystery: Real Gold vs Pyrite
slides.content:
How can density identify "Fool's Gold"?

• Sample Mass: 38.6 g, Volume: 2.0 mL
• Calculated Density: 38.6 / 2.0 = 19.3 g/cm³
• Pure Gold density is exactly 19.3 g/cm³.
• Iron Pyrite (Fool's Gold) density is only 5.0 g/cm³.
• Conclusion: The sample is genuine pure gold!

slides.title: Classroom Calculation Check
slides.content:
A rock has a mass of 120 grams and displaces 40 mL of water. What is its density?
A) 3.0 g/cm³
B) 0.33 g/cm³
C) 4,800 g/cm³
D) 80 g/cm³

Correct Answer: A (120 g / 40 mL = 3.0 g/cm³)

customLessons.title: States of Matter
objectives: Describe the Kinetic Molecular Theory of matter (particle arrangement, motion, and attraction).
Compare the physical and molecular properties of solids, liquids, and gases.
Explain the fourth state of matter (plasma) and where it is found in the cosmos.
customLessons.content:
All matter is made of tiny, constantly moving particles (atoms and molecules). The kinetic energy of these particles determines the state of matter.

In solids, particles are packed tightly in fixed, orderly arrangements; they vibrate in place and have strong intermolecular attractions, giving solids definite shape and volume.

In liquids, particles have more energy, slide past one another fluidly, and have moderate attraction; liquids have definite volume but take the shape of their container.

In gases, particles possess high kinetic energy, fly freely at high speeds, and have negligible attraction; gases expand to fill the entire volume and shape of their container.

Plasma is an ionized gas of free electrons and positive ions formed at ultra-high temperatures. It is found in stars, lightning bolts, auroras, and neon lights, making it the most abundant state of matter in the universe.

slides.title: States of Matter & Molecular Physics
slides.content:
Grade 5 — Term 1 Science

Examine matter at the particulate level: solids, liquids, gases, and high-energy plasma.

slides.title: Kinetic Molecular Theory (KMT)
slides.content:
Fundamental Principles of KMT:
1. All matter consists of extremely tiny particles (atoms/molecules)
2. Particles are in constant, random motion
3. Higher temperature = Higher average kinetic energy and velocity
4. Attractive forces hold particles together unless overcome by heat

slides.title: Solid vs Liquid vs Gas at Particle Level
slides.content:
Comparative Particle Matrix:
• Solid: Rigid lattice, tightly packed, vibrates in place, definite shape and volume
• Liquid: Close together, free to slide past one another, definite volume, takes container shape
• Gas: Far apart, high-speed chaotic collisions, no definite shape, no definite volume (compressible)
slides.mediaUrl:
Solid: Low energy, locked lattice
Liquid: Medium energy, sliding particles
Gas: High energy, high velocity collisions
Plasma: Extreme energy, stripped ions & electrons

slides.title: Plasma — The Fourth State of Matter
slides.content:
Beyond gas lies Plasma:
• When gas is heated to super-high temperatures, electrons are stripped away from nuclei
• Consists of positively charged ions and free electrons
• Conducts electricity and responds strongly to magnetic fields
• Found in: The Sun and stars (99% of visible universe), lightning bolts, neon signs, and auroras

slides.title: Thinking Challenge: Tire Pressure
slides.content:
Why does automobile tire pressure increase significantly after driving for hours on a hot asphalt highway?
A) More air entered the tire from the road
B) Heat increased the kinetic energy of air molecules inside, causing more frequent, forceful collisions against tire walls
C) The rubber contracted into a smaller size
D) The tire absorbed water vapor

Correct Answer: B (Higher temperature increases gas pressure!)

customLessons.title: Changes in Matter
objectives: Classify changes in matter as endothermic (heat-absorbing) or exothermic (heat-releasing).
Explain energy transfers during phase changes (melting, vaporization, condensation, freezing).
Investigate everyday chemical changes such as cellular respiration, digestion, and combustion.
customLessons.content:
Changes in matter are accompanied by energy transformations. Heat energy flows between substances and their surroundings.

Endothermic changes absorb heat from the surroundings. When ice melts or water boils, particles absorb thermal energy to break intermolecular attractions. As a result, the immediate surroundings feel cooler.

Exothermic changes release heat into the surroundings. When water freezes or water vapor condenses, particles release thermal energy to lock into place. Combustion (burning wood or gas) releases enormous amounts of thermal energy and light.

Biological systems rely on continuous changes in matter: our digestive system breaks food into glucose molecules, which our cells burn with oxygen during cellular respiration to release metabolic energy (ATP).

slides.title: Changes in Matter & Energy Transfers
slides.content:
Grade 5 — Term 1 Science

Track heat energy flow: endothermic (absorbing heat) vs exothermic (releasing heat).

slides.title: Endothermic vs Exothermic Reactions
slides.content:
Direction of Thermal Energy Flow:
• Endothermic (Heat Enters):
  - System absorbs heat from surroundings
  - Surroundings feel COLD
  - Examples: Ice melting, water boiling, cold packs, photosynthesis
• Exothermic (Heat Exits):
  - System releases heat to surroundings
  - Surroundings feel HOT
  - Examples: Fire burning, fireworks, hand warmers, freezing

slides.title: Phase Changes & Latent Heat
slides.content:
Thermal shifts during phase transitions:
• Melting & Boiling are ENDOTHERMIC: Heat energy breaks particle bonds
• Freezing & Condensation are EXOTHERMIC: Heat energy is released as bonds form
• While changing state, temperature stays constant at the plateau point!
slides.mediaUrl:
Solid (-10°C) -> Add heat -> Melts at 0°C
Liquid (0°C to 100°C) -> Add heat -> Boils at 100°C
Gas (>100°C) -> Freely expanding vapor

slides.title: Biological Energy Changes: Cellular Respiration
slides.content:
Energy in living cells:
Glucose (C6H12O6) + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + Energy (ATP)

• Chemical transformation in mitochondria
• Exothermic biological reaction providing body warmth and muscular movement

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Cold Rubbing Alcohol
slides.content:
When you apply rubbing alcohol to your skin, why does your arm immediately feel cold?
A) Alcohol freezes on your skin
B) Alcohol absorbs heat from your skin as it rapidly evaporates (an endothermic change for the liquid)
C) Alcohol turns into ice
D) Alcohol chemically reacts to produce cold acid

Correct Answer: B (Evaporative cooling absorbs your body heat!)

customLessons.title: Scientific Investigation of Matter
objectives: Formulate testable hypotheses, identify independent, dependent, and controlled variables.
Design and conduct a fair test investigation on the physical and chemical properties of matter.
Collect quantitative experimental data, construct data tables, and draw valid conclusions.
customLessons.content:
Science advances through systematic inquiry. The scientific method provides a structured approach: Problem -> Hypothesis -> Controlled Experiment -> Data Collection -> Analysis -> Conclusion.

A fair test requires controlling variables:
- Independent Variable (IV): the single condition the scientist deliberately changes (e.g., water temperature).
- Dependent Variable (DV): the observable outcome that is measured (e.g., time taken for sugar to dissolve).
- Controlled Variables (CV): all other factors kept strictly identical (volume of water, amount of sugar, stirring speed).

Replicating trials (running at least 3 trials) ensures results are reliable, objective, and reproducible.

slides.title: Scientific Investigation of Matter
slides.content:
Grade 5 — Term 1 Science

Learn the scientific method: formulating hypotheses, controlling variables, and analyzing fair tests.

slides.title: The Scientific Method Steps
slides.content:
Systematic Inquiry Cycle:
1. Question / Problem: What are we investigating?
2. Hypothesis: Testable "If... then... because..." prediction
3. Controlled Experiment: Designing the fair test
4. Data Gathering: Quantitative measurements (numbers) and qualitative notes (observations)
5. Analysis & Conclusion: Does evidence support the hypothesis?

slides.title: Variables in a Fair Test
slides.content:
Understanding the three variable types:
• Independent Variable (IV): The ONE factor you change (e.g., Water Temperature: 20°C, 50°C, 80°C)
• Dependent Variable (DV): What you measure (e.g., Dissolving time in seconds)
• Controlled Variables (CV): Kept EXACTLY equal (volume of water, mass of solute, stirring rate)
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Set up 3 identical beakers
Step 2: Add 100mL water at 20°C, 50°C, 80°C
Step 3: Add 10g sugar simultaneously
Step 4: Time until complete dissolution

slides.title: Data Tables, Replications, & Graphs
slides.content:
Why run 3 experimental trials?

• Human error and slight timing variations happen.
• Calculating the average of Trials 1, 2, and 3 produces trustworthy scientific data:
  Average = (T1 + T2 + T3) / 3
• Plotting temperature vs time reveals the inverse dissolving curve.

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Variable Identification
slides.content:
In an experiment testing which brand of paper towel absorbs the most water, what is the Independent Variable?
A) The volume of water absorbed
B) The brand of paper towel used
C) The temperature of the room
D) The size of the measuring cup

Correct Answer: B (The brand is the single factor deliberately tested and changed!)

customLessons.title: Changes in Matter
objectives: Describe factors affecting the rate of changes in matter (temperature, surface area, concentration, catalysts).
Explain the Law of Conservation of Mass in both open and closed systems.
Analyze natural biochemical decay, fermentation, and rust formation processes.
customLessons.content:
The rate at which matter undergoes physical and chemical transformations depends on specific kinetic factors:
- Temperature: Higher temperatures increase particle collisions and reaction speed.
- Surface Area: Crushing a solid into powder exposes more particles to reactants, speeding up the reaction.
- Concentration: More reactant particles in a given volume increases the frequency of collisions.
- Catalysts: Substances like enzymes that accelerate reactions without being consumed.

The Law of Conservation of Mass states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed in any physical or chemical change. The total mass of reactants always equals the total mass of products.

In open systems, gases (like carbon dioxide from vinegar and baking soda) escape into the air, making it seem like mass was lost. In a sealed closed container, the measured mass remains exactly identical before and after the reaction.

slides.title: Changes in Matter: Reaction Kinetics
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Science

Explore factors controlling reaction rates and master the Law of Conservation of Mass.

slides.title: Four Factors Affecting Reaction Rates
slides.content:
How to speed up or slow down changes in matter:
1. Temperature: Heat increases molecular speed and collision frequency
2. Surface Area: Powder reacts faster than solid blocks
3. Concentration: More reactant molecules per volume = more collisions
4. Catalysts: Biological enzymes or chemical agents that lower activation energy

slides.title: The Law of Conservation of Mass
slides.content:
Fundamental Law of Chemistry:
Mass of Reactants = Mass of Products

• Atoms are neither created nor destroyed during chemical reactions; they are merely rearranged.
• In open systems: Gases escape into atmosphere, appearing to lose mass.
• In closed systems: Sealed mass before reaction = sealed mass after reaction!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Weigh flask with vinegar + balloon with baking soda
Step 2: Tip balloon to start reaction
Step 3: Gas inflates balloon inside closed system
Step 4: Re-weigh: Mass remains exactly unchanged!

slides.title: Everyday Biochemical Changes
slides.content:
Real-world reactions in action:
• Fermentation: Yeast converts sugar into alcohol and CO2 gas (makes bread dough rise!)
• Food Spoilage: Bacterial enzymes oxidize organic food molecules
• Refrigeration: Lowers temperature to dramatically slow decay reaction rates

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Fireplace Mass Mystery
slides.content:
A 10kg wooden log burns down to 500g of ash in a fireplace. Has mass been destroyed?
A) Yes, 9.5kg of matter was permanently destroyed
B) No, 9.5kg of mass escaped as carbon dioxide gas, water vapor, and smoke into the atmosphere
C) The fire absorbed the mass
D) Ash is denser than wood

Correct Answer: B (Conservation of Mass applies; gas escaped into the open system!)

customLessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
objectives: Compare physical and chemical changes at the atomic, molecular, and energetic levels.
Identify reactants, products, and energy transformations in chemical reactions.
Evaluate how understanding physical and chemical changes enables food preservation and material protection.
customLessons.content:
At the microscopic scale, physical changes rearrange molecules without altering their intramolecular chemical bonds. Liquid water and ice are both composed of H2O molecules.

Chemical reactions break chemical bonds between reactant atoms and form new bonds to create products with completely novel chemical formulas and properties:
Reactants -> Products

Energy is involved in bond reorganization: breaking bonds requires energy input, while creating new bonds releases energy.

Human civilization applies these principles: canning and pickling alter acidity to prevent chemical decay; galvanizing iron coats it with zinc to sacrifice-protect it against oxidation; refining crude oil uses fractional distillation (physical separation) followed by catalytic cracking (chemical change).

slides.title: Physical & Chemical Changes: Deep Dive
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Science

Examine atomic rearrangements, chemical equations, and industrial applications.

slides.title: Atomic Realities: Bonds & Molecules
slides.content:
What happens to atoms?
• Physical Change: Molecules stay intact; only spacing and orientation shift (e.g., Ice -> Water -> Steam is still H2O)
• Chemical Change: Covalent or ionic bonds break; atoms recombine into new molecular structures with unique formulas:
CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + Heat

slides.title: Reactants, Products, & Energy Shifts
slides.content:
Key Anatomy of a Reaction:
• Reactants: Starting chemical compounds on the left
• Products: Newly formed chemical compounds on the right
• Activation Energy: Minimum energy required to trigger reaction
• Bond breaking = Energy absorbed
• Bond formation = Energy released
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Reactants collide with sufficient energy
Step 2: Old chemical bonds break
Step 3: Atoms rearrange
Step 4: New bonds form into Products

slides.title: Industrial & Everyday Technologies
slides.content:
Harnessing changes in materials:
• Galvanization: Coating steel with zinc prevents oxidation
• Pickling & Canning: Acidity denatures bacterial enzymes chemically
• Water Desalination: Physical evaporation followed by condensation produces drinking water
• Polymerization: Chemical bonding creates synthetic fibers and medical polymers

slides.title: Quick Quiz: Molecular Recognition
slides.content:
Which event involves breaking and forming chemical bonds to produce a completely new substance?
A) Melting a block of copper metal into liquid copper
B) Dissolving salt in warm water
C) The combustion of gasoline in a car engine producing CO2 and H2O
D) Shredding paper into fine confetti

Correct Answer: C (Combustion is a profound chemical reaction!)

customLessons.title: Mixtures and Solutions
objectives: Differentiate homogeneous mixtures (solutions) from heterogeneous mixtures (suspensions and colloids).
Identify the components of a solution: solute and solvent.
Explain factors affecting solubility and demonstrate the Tyndall Effect.
customLessons.content:
A mixture consists of two or more substances physically combined in any proportion where each substance retains its individual chemical identity.

Heterogeneous mixtures have non-uniform composition and visible distinct phases (e.g., fruit salad, oil and water, muddy water).

Homogeneous mixtures (solutions) have a completely uniform appearance throughout. The substance that dissolves is the solute; the dissolving medium is the solvent (water is called the 'universal solvent').

Colloids have intermediate particle sizes that do not settle out and scatter beams of light (Tyndall Effect), such as milk, mayonnaise, and fog. Suspensions have large particles that eventually settle to the bottom if left undisturbed, such as calamine lotion or river sediment.

Solubility factors: Solutes dissolve faster with heating (for solids), stirring (agitation), and crushing (reducing particle size).

slides.title: Mixtures and Solutions
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Science

Classify matter: homogeneous solutions, heterogeneous mixtures, colloids, and suspensions.

slides.title: Heterogeneous vs Homogeneous
slides.content:
The Big Division:
• Heterogeneous: Non-uniform; visible separate phases
  - Examples: Halo-halo, oil and vinegar, granite, salad
• Homogeneous (Solutions): Uniform throughout; single visible phase
  - Solute: Substance dissolved (lesser amount, e.g., salt, sugar)
  - Solvent: Dissolving medium (greater amount, e.g., water, alcohol)

slides.title: The Spectrum: Solution, Colloid, Suspension
slides.content:
Particle Size Comparison:
• Solution (<1 nm): Salt water, air, brass (never settles, clear)
• Colloid (1–1000 nm): Milk, gelatin, fog, mayonnaise (does not settle, cloudy)
• Suspension (>1000 nm): Muddy water, calamine, cough syrup (settles upon standing, must shake before use)
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Shine flashlight through water (invisible beam)
Step 2: Shine flashlight through salt solution (invisible beam)
Step 3: Shine flashlight through diluted milk (bright beam!)
Step 4: Confirm Tyndall Effect in colloid

slides.title: Factors Affecting Rate of Dissolving
slides.content:
How to speed up solid solute dissolution:
1. Temperature: Increases molecular kinetic collisions
2. Agitation (Stirring): Brings fresh solvent molecules into contact with solute
3. Surface Area (Crushing): Exposes more solute particles to solvent

slides.title: Quick Quiz: The Tyndall Effect
slides.content:
A teacher shines a laser pointer through two beakers. In Beaker A, the beam is invisible. In Beaker B, the beam glows brightly through the liquid. What are Beakers A and B?
A) Beaker A is a colloid; Beaker B is a true solution
B) Beaker A is a true solution; Beaker B is a colloid showing the Tyndall Effect
C) Both are suspensions
D) Both are pure water

Correct Answer: B (Colloidal particles scatter light beams!)

customLessons.title: Separation of Mixtures
objectives: Explain principles behind physical separation methods: filtration, decantation, evaporation, magnetic separation, sieving, and distillation.
Select and execute appropriate separation techniques based on the physical properties of mixture components.
Apply separation processes to municipal water purification and scrap metal recycling.
customLessons.content:
Because substances in a mixture are only physically combined, they can be separated back into pure components using differences in their physical properties (particle size, density, boiling point, magnetic attraction).

Techniques:
- Decantation: Pouring off a less dense liquid layer from a settled denser sediment or immiscible liquid (e.g., oil from water).
- Filtration: Passing a mixture through a porous barrier (filter paper) to trap insoluble solid residue while liquid filtrate passes through.
- Evaporation: Heating a solution until the liquid solvent vaporizes into air, leaving solid solute crystals behind (e.g., harvesting sea salt).
- Magnetic Separation: Using magnets to extract magnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) from non-magnetic mixtures (e.g., scrap metal sorting).
- Sieving & Winnowing: Separating particles by size using a mesh screen, or by density using wind currents (e.g., separating rice grain from chaff).
- Distillation: Vaporizing a liquid and condensing its vapor back into pure liquid in a separate container, separating liquids with different boiling points or purifying freshwater from saltwater.

Real-world applications: Water treatment plants use screening, sedimentation, filtration, and chlorination to provide safe drinking water to cities.

slides.title: Separation of Mixtures
slides.content:
Grade 6 — Term 1 Science

Techniques for purifying matter: filtration, evaporation, decantation, distillation, and magnetic separation.

slides.title: Common Separation Techniques
slides.content:
Exploiting physical differences:
• Decantation: Pouring off top liquid from settled sediment (density difference)
• Filtration: Using filter paper to trap solid residue from liquid filtrate (particle size)
• Evaporation: Heating solution to leave dry solute behind (boiling point difference)
• Magnetic Separation: Pulling out iron/steel with magnets (magnetic attraction)

slides.title: Distillation: Collecting the Solvent
slides.content:
How simple distillation works:
1. Boiling flask heats saltwater solution
2. Water vapor rises, leaving salt behind
3. Steam passes through water-cooled condenser
4. Pure condensed liquid water drips into receiving flask
• Used to desalinate ocean water and produce distilled water!
slides.mediaUrl:
Step 1: Heat saltwater to boiling (100°C)
Step 2: Steam travels into Liebig condenser
Step 3: Cold water cools steam back to liquid
Step 4: Collect pure distilled freshwater

slides.title: Municipal Water Treatment Plants
slides.content:
How river water becomes safe tap water:
• Coagulation & Flocculation: Alum binds dirt particles together
• Sedimentation: Heavy flocs settle to tank floor
• Sand/Charcoal Filtration: Traps microscopic suspended particles
• Chlorination: Kills harmful bacteria and pathogens

slides.title: Classroom Separation Challenge
slides.content:
How would you separate a mixture of sand, salt, and iron filings?
A) Heat it until everything burns
B) 1: Magnet extracts iron; 2: Add water to dissolve salt; 3: Filter out sand; 4: Evaporate water to recover salt
C) Throw it away
D) Freeze it into ice

Correct Answer: B (A logical 4-step physical separation protocol!)
